node.title: Ecosystem: Structure and function; Productivity; Decomposition; Energy flow – different

questions.stem: The standing crop of an ecosystem is best described as
options: the rate of production of organic matter per unit area per year
the mass of living organisms present in a unit area at a given time
the total dead organic matter lying on the ground
the energy captured by producers each day
questions.explanation: Standing crop is a measure of the living biomass (or number) of the organisms in a unit area at a particular moment. It is a quantity at one time, not a rate, which is how it differs from productivity.

optionRationale.1: This describes a rate, which is productivity, not a standing crop.
optionRationale.3: Dead organic matter is detritus, not the living standing crop.
optionRationale.4: Energy captured per day is a rate of energy flow, not a stock of living organisms.

questions.stem: In the grazing food chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, the primary consumer is the
questions.explanation: Primary consumers are the herbivores that feed directly on producers. Here the grasshopper eats grass, so it is the primary consumer at the second trophic level. The frog is the secondary consumer and the snake the tertiary consumer.

optionRationale.1: Grass is the producer at the first trophic level.
optionRationale.2: The frog feeds on the grasshopper, so it is a secondary consumer.
optionRationale.4: The snake feeds on the frog, so it is a tertiary consumer.

questions.objective: Identify trophic levels in a grazing food chain

questions.stem: The detritus food chain begins with
questions.explanation: In the detritus food chain the first link is dead organic matter, which is eaten by detritivores and decomposers such as fungi and bacteria. The grazing food chain, in contrast, starts with living green plants.

optionRationale.2: A chain that begins with green plants is the grazing food chain.
optionRationale.3: Herbivores feeding on living plants belong to the grazing food chain.
optionRationale.4: Carnivores are higher links, not the start of any chain.

questions.objective: State the starting point of the detritus food chain

questions.stem: In a terrestrial ecosystem such as a forest, the pyramid of biomass is generally upright because
options: the number of individual producers always exceeds the number of consumers
energy flows from the consumers back to the producers
decomposers have the largest biomass at the base
the biomass of producers is much greater than that of each higher trophic level
questions.explanation: On land the producers are large and long-lived plants whose total mass is far greater than that of herbivores, which in turn outweigh the carnivores. So the biomass falls at each higher level and the pyramid is upright.

optionRationale.1: Numbers can be misleading, as one tree supports many insects; the pyramid of biomass depends on mass, not number.
optionRationale.2: Energy never flows back to producers; flow is one-way.
optionRationale.3: Decomposers are not placed as a base level in a pyramid of biomass.

questions.objective: Explain the upright pyramid of biomass on land

questions.stem: Energy flow in an ecosystem is unidirectional because
options: heat lost in respiration can be reused by plants in photosynthesis
consumers return their energy to producers through excretion
energy captured by autotrophs does not revert to the sun, and energy passing to herbivores does not come back to the producers
producers receive a fixed share of energy from decomposers each year
questions.explanation: Solar energy is trapped by producers and passes forward to consumers, losing heat at every step. This heat cannot be used again by plants and energy does not flow backward, so the flow is one-way, unlike nutrients, which cycle.

optionRationale.1: Heat lost in respiration is dissipated and plants cannot use it in photosynthesis.
optionRationale.2: Excretion returns nutrients, not usable energy, to producers.
optionRationale.4: Producers get their energy from sunlight, not from decomposers.

questions.objective: Explain why energy flow is one-way

questions.stem: In a lake, the gross primary productivity is 2000 kcal m$^{-2}$ yr$^{-1}$ and plants use 35 per cent of it in respiration. The net primary productivity is
questions.explanation: Net primary productivity equals gross primary productivity minus respiratory losses. Respiration uses 35 per cent of 2000, which is 700. So NPP = 2000 − 700 = 1300 kcal per square metre per year.

optionRationale.2: 700 is the amount used in respiration, not what remains.
optionRationale.3: This subtracts 35 units instead of 35 per cent of GPP.
optionRationale.4: This adds the respiratory loss instead of subtracting it.

questions.objective: Compute NPP from GPP and respiration

questions.stem: Producers of a grassland fix 50000 kJ of energy. Using the ten per cent law, the energy available to the tertiary consumer, which is at the fourth trophic level, is
questions.explanation: Each transfer passes about 10 per cent of the energy on. Producers 50000 kJ give 5000 kJ to the primary consumer, 500 kJ to the secondary consumer and 50 kJ to the tertiary consumer, which is the fourth level.

optionRationale.1: 5000 kJ reaches only the primary consumer, the second level.
optionRationale.3: 500 kJ reaches only the secondary consumer, the third level.
optionRationale.4: 5 kJ would be the fifth level, one step too far.

questions.objective: Apply the ten per cent law over three transfers

questions.stem: In the food chain phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → large fish, the large fish obtain 8 kJ of energy. If the ten per cent law holds at every step, the energy fixed by the phytoplankton was
questions.explanation: Going backwards, each step needs ten times the energy of the next one. Large fish 8 kJ means small fish 80 kJ, zooplankton 800 kJ and phytoplankton 8000 kJ. Three transfers means a factor of 10 cubed, which is 1000.

optionRationale.2: 800 kJ is only the zooplankton level.
optionRationale.3: 80 kJ is only the small fish level.
optionRationale.4: 80000 kJ multiplies by ten one time too many.

questions.objective: Work backwards through a food chain using the ten per cent law

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes standing crop from productivity?
options: Standing crop is a quantity measured at one moment, whereas productivity is a rate of organic matter formed per unit area per unit time
Standing crop is measured in grams per square metre per year, whereas productivity is measured in grams per square metre
Standing crop is the energy lost in respiration, whereas productivity is the energy that remains
Both are rates and are measured in the same units
questions.explanation: Standing crop is the stock of living material at a point in time, expressed per unit area. Productivity is the rate at which biomass or energy is produced, so it carries a time unit such as g per square metre per year.

optionRationale.2: The units are reversed in this statement.
optionRationale.3: Respiratory loss is the difference between GPP and NPP, not a standing crop.
optionRationale.4: Standing crop has no time unit, so it is not a rate.

questions.objective: Distinguish stock from rate in ecosystem ecology

questions.stem: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk, match the organism in List-I with its role in List-II.
questions.explanation: Grass makes food, so it is the producer at level one. The grasshopper eats grass and is a primary consumer at level two. The frog eats the grasshopper and is at level three. The hawk, at the end of the chain, is the fifth level.

optionRationale.1: This pairs 'Grass' with 'Primary consumer at the second trophic level', which describes 'Grasshopper'.
optionRationale.2: This pairs 'Frog' with 'Top carnivore at the fifth trophic level', which describes 'Hawk'.
optionRationale.3: This pairs 'Grass' with 'Secondary consumer at the third trophic level', which describes 'Frog'.

right: I. Secondary consumer at the third trophic level
II. Producer at the first trophic level
III. Top carnivore at the fifth trophic level
IV. Primary consumer at the second trophic level

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The annual net primary productivity of the whole biosphere is about 170 billion tons of dry organic matter.
Reason (R): The oceans, which cover about 70 per cent of the earth's surface, contribute more to this productivity than the land does.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The biosphere's net primary productivity is about 170 billion tons of dry matter, so A is true. Although the oceans cover about 70 per cent of the surface, their share is only about 55 billion tons, less than the land contributes. So R is false.

optionRationale.1: R is false, so the pair cannot both be true.
optionRationale.2: R is false, so the pair cannot both be true.
optionRationale.4: A is true, so this option is wrong.

questions.objective: Compare land and ocean contributions to productivity

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Hot deserts have the highest net primary productivity among all terrestrial ecosystems.
Reason (R): Availability of water, temperature and soil nutrients are factors that influence primary productivity.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Deserts have low productivity because water is scarce, so A is false. R is a true statement, since solar radiation, temperature, moisture and soil nutrients control how much organic matter producers can make.

optionRationale.1: A is false, so this cannot be right.
optionRationale.2: A is false, so this cannot be right.
optionRationale.3: R is true, so this option is wrong.

questions.stem: Match the term in List-I with its meaning in List-II.
questions.explanation: Standing crop is a stock of living organisms at one time. Primary productivity is the rate of making organic matter by producers, secondary productivity is the same rate for consumers, and detritus is dead plant and animal material.

optionRationale.1: This pairs 'Standing crop' with 'Rate of formation of organic matter by producers', which describes 'Primary productivity'.
optionRationale.3: This pairs 'Secondary productivity' with 'Dead remains of plants and animals including faecal matter', which describes 'Detritus'.
optionRationale.4: This pairs 'Standing crop' with 'Rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers', which describes 'Secondary productivity'.

right: I. Rate of formation of organic matter by producers
II. Dead remains of plants and animals including faecal matter
III. Mass of living organisms per unit area at a given time
IV. Rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about productivity.
A. Gross primary productivity minus respiratory losses gives net primary productivity.
B. Net primary productivity is the biomass available for consumption by heterotrophs.
C. Secondary productivity is the rate of formation of new organic matter by producers.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: NPP is GPP minus respiration, and it is the plant biomass that remains for herbivores and decomposers. So A and B are correct. Secondary productivity refers to new organic matter formed by consumers, not producers, so C is wrong.

optionRationale.1: C is wrong, since producers show primary productivity.
optionRationale.2: C is wrong, and A is correct.
optionRationale.4: C is wrong, so not all statements are correct.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about decomposition.
A. Detritus rich in nitrogen and water-soluble substances decomposes more slowly.
B. Decomposition is slower under anaerobic conditions.
C. Chitin and lignin slow down the decomposition of detritus.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Decomposition is an oxygen-requiring process, so lack of oxygen slows it. Lignin and chitin resist breakdown. Nitrogen-rich and water-soluble detritus is decomposed faster and not slower, so statement A is wrong.

optionRationale.1: A is wrong; such detritus decomposes faster.
optionRationale.3: A is wrong, since nitrogen and soluble substances speed decomposition.
optionRationale.4: A is wrong, so not all statements are correct.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on factors affecting decomposition
